passage.text:
School libraries notice
The school libraries team needs helpers on Saturday. Bring gloves and arrive before nine.

Message from a friend
I have booked the reading corners session for Tuesday, but I may arrive late. Please start without me and save a place.

Information sign
Visitors to the school libraries may use the tools, but they must return them before leaving.

Short announcement
The students meeting has moved from Room 2 to Room 4 because the first room is being painted.

Notice for members
Members can borrow one reading corners guide for a week. Ask at the desk if you need another copy.

passage.text: The people below want to choose from school libraries and reading spaces. Decide which option is most suitable.

passage.label: A
passage.text: Lunchtime book circle with audio — A weekly book circle held in the library at midday every Wednesday. Members choose a story together, listen to audio editions on shared headphones and chat about the plot over sandwiches. New members can join mid-term without booking, no homework is set between meetings, and everyone leaves with a short list of books to try next.

passage.label: B
passage.text: Silent homework corner after lessons — A calm study area open from the final bell until five o'clock on school days. The corner has individual desks, power sockets and free Wi-Fi, and mobile phones must stay switched off. Students may bring drinks but not food, and a helper quietly collects books that need returning to the shelves.

passage.label: C
passage.text: Saturday storytelling hour for young pupils — An hour of picture-book storytelling held on Saturday mornings for children aged six to eight. A volunteer reads aloud, families join together and every child takes home a bookmark with the story list. No previous library membership is needed, and the session repeats each month so families can choose the date that suits them best.

passage.label: D
passage.text: Online ebook club from home — A digital reading club where members borrow ebooks through the school app and share short reviews on a weekly message board. Everything happens online, so there are no travel costs, and the club stays open during holidays. A parent account is required for members under twelve, and new titles arrive each month.

passage.label: E
passage.text: Exam revision zone with tutor drop-ins — A supervised revision space for older students sitting their final summer exams. Subject tutors drop in each Tuesday and Thursday afternoon, and printed revision guides cover English, maths and science. Attendance is free, but the zone is reserved for pupils who have already returned all borrowed books, so the room stays calm and well-stocked.

passage.label: F
passage.text: Library helper badge programme — A volunteer programme where students sort returned shelves, repair torn pages and guide new pupils to the catalogue. Helpers attend a short training session, meet other volunteers in the library kitchen and earn a badge after six weeks. The role suits pupils who can arrive ten minutes early on their chosen weekday.

passage.label: G
passage.text: Reading corner makeover team — A small team that redesigns the library reading corner, choosing cushions, posters and a new display shelf. The project runs for one term on Thursday afternoons, and members must attend most sessions to finish the design. Spaces are limited, and previous art skills are welcome but not required.

passage.label: H
passage.text: Creative writing circle in the studio — A writing circle that meets in the library's upstairs studio, where pupils compose short stories and poems on shared laptops. Finished work appears in the school magazine each term, and an editor gives friendly feedback. The circle takes eight members and opens twice a year, in September and January.

questions.prompt: Arif is in his final year and revising for summer exams in English and maths. He wants free tutor help on weekday afternoons and printed study guides, but he still owes two library books that he plans to return this week.

Chloe wants a quiet place to finish homework after the last lesson without being disturbed. She needs a desk with power for her laptop and free internet, and she wants to keep her phone off while she works.

Nina enjoys writing short stories at home and would like feedback from someone who reads carefully. She can manage one fixed meeting each term, wants her work published somewhere, and prefers a small group in a quiet room.

Rosa has no free time after school because of football practice, but she is free in the middle of the day. She wants to listen to stories rather than read long pages, and she prefers activities where she can start without booking.

Daniel's family has no car and he lives far from the school library. He wants to borrow ebooks on his tablet, share his thoughts with other readers weekly, and keep reading during the holidays. His mother is happy to create an account for him.

passage.text: When the students in our town started a school libraries project, few residents expected it to grow so quickly. At first, the organisers met in a small room and planned one simple activity involving reading corners. They soon discovered that people were more willing to join when they could see a clear benefit for the neighbourhood. The organisers therefore published a short timetable and invited local businesses to offer practical help.

The project was not completely easy. Some volunteers were worried that the work would take too much time, while others wanted to change the plan every week. The team solved this by giving each person one small responsibility and reviewing the results together. This made the project feel manageable, and it also meant that new volunteers could contribute without special experience.

Looking back, the organiser says the most important lesson was not the final result but the way people learned to cooperate. The group still has problems, especially when the weather affects outdoor work, yet members now discuss solutions rather than blaming one another. For this reason, the project has become a useful example of how a modest local idea can create lasting connections.

passage.text: The school library team wanted more students to use its reading spaces. (16) The team first compared the busy library with the quieter study room. Before the work began, books were mixed together and the only table was often reserved for meetings. Students said they needed both quiet study space and somewhere to share ideas. This evidence helped the school separate furniture problems from requests for more books and better online access. They moved shelves to create a quiet corner and placed a clear sign near the entrance. (17) The new sign helped students understand the purpose of the corner. The librarian sorted requests by age and subject, then compared them with the catalogue. The school bought novels, reference books and licences for two useful databases. The catalogue also showed which older titles were still borrowed, so useful books were not removed simply because they looked old. The librarian then asked pupils which books and digital resources they needed. (18) Pupils mentioned novels, information books and online reference material. Furniture was moved so younger pupils could read near the window while older students worked near power sockets. A notice explained which areas should remain quiet. Power sockets were positioned away from the quietest seats, reducing noise when students charged devices. A borrowing card explained opening hours and showed where returned books should go. (19) The card prevented returned books from being left on the wrong shelf. The timetable included homework support after lessons, but reading clubs used the shared area on Wednesdays. Staff also taught students how to search the digital catalogue. The arrangement gave every group a clear purpose and stopped homework support from disturbing readers. Reading-club volunteers prepared recommendation cards for students who wanted help choosing. (20) By the end of term, the library felt easier to use without becoming silent or unfriendly. The recommendations supported choice rather than giving every reader the same list. A termly survey showed that borrowing rose without reducing study time. The librarian plans to review popular titles and change the layout whenever students need a different balance.

parts.passageTitle: Part 5 – The School Library Reading Club

passage.text: The librarian checks (21) ........ books have been returned before closing each evening. Students can ask (22) ........ a title or search the digital catalogue from any computer. The quiet corner is kept clear (23) ........ pupils can study without interruption from group work. Volunteers place new books (24) ........ the display shelf after they are recorded in the system. Reading clubs meet (25) ........ the final lesson on Fridays, giving members a full hour for discussion. The library welcomes (26) ........ student who wants to read or work in a calm environment. The reading club chooses a title to discuss each month. Members explain what they enjoyed about a character or an idea. The librarian records useful recommendations for other readers. New students can join even if they have missed the first meeting of the term. Volunteers then return every book to its correct shelf and check the catalogue afterwards. This routine keeps the library organised and makes it easy for students to find what they need. The librarian also keeps a list where students can suggest new titles.

parts.passageTitle: Part 6 – Borrowing Rules at the School Library

passage.text: The librarian records (27) ........ books students borrow most often during each term. Pupils can search (28) ........ the digital catalogue before asking for help at the front desk. They may study quietly in the reading area, (29) ........ they must leave the shelves tidy after removing a book. Volunteers prevent returned books (30) ........ being lost in the wrong section before staff can check them in. The library is a place (31) ........ students of all ages can read together in a calm space. Everyone remembers (32) ........ bring their library card when borrowing any item. Students should check whether the library is open before arriving after school. They may borrow a book for two weeks unless another reader has reserved it. Quiet areas are for individual work, but the shared table is available for group discussion. Pupils can ask for help if the catalogue search does not find what they need. The librarian keeps a list where students can suggest new titles for the collection.
